title: Birth and family; move from Michigan to Harrison
description: Gertrude Hudson gives her name, maiden name Dawson, and birth date of December 20, 1899 in Menominee, Michigan. She explains how her family traveled by Northern Pacific railroad to Harrison, Idaho in 1900-1901, where her father found mill work, and describes her parents' Wisconsin and German origins.

title: Childhood in Harrison; schooling; family games
description: She describes Harrison's growth and decline as a lumber town, playing baseball, fishing and boating with her brothers, and attending grade school and high school in Harrison. She notes her older brother's studies in forestry and that her parents expected both sons and daughters to pursue education equally.

title: First teaching jobs; flu epidemic; boarding with Sanders family
description: Hudson recalls starting to teach at 18 after finishing high school in three years, with school closures during the flu epidemic. She taught at Black Rock for three years, boarding with the Sanders family who had known her since childhood, and took the train home to Harrison on weekends.

title: Teaching moves; favorite subjects; pupils
description: She covers her moves to teach in Greenwood, Fernwood and Harrison, and describes her pupils including farm children and two handicapped Italian children. History and geography were her favorite subjects, and she taught children about local rivers, flooding, soil and contour plowing.

title: University of Idaho; father's mill job; master's work
description: Hudson describes starting at the University of Idaho in 1924, taking heavy course loads, and spending a summer at the lumber camp where her father managed the mill. She accumulated extra credits, nearly finished her master's degree, and accepted a teaching fellowship at her father's urging.

title: Teaching in Portland; move to Lewiston; tonsil surgery
description: After her fellowship she taught in Portland where her family had relocated, then moved to Lewiston after tonsil surgery, teaching fifth grade and elementary grades. She taught in Lewiston for twenty years at normal school and training school.

title: Marriage at fifty; husband's work; keeping her career
description: Hudson explains that she married at Thanksgiving 1949 at about age 50, having met her husband through friends in Lewiston, and moved to Portland. She describes insisting on continuing to teach after marriage and hiring a housekeeper so she would not be exhausted on weekends.

title: Single life; family support; Depression travels
description: She reflects on never feeling out of place as a single woman, her family's encouragement of her independence, and working through the Depression. She describes summer trips to Yellowstone, Glacier, Rocky Mountain National Park and New England with friends.

title: Depression economy; salary cuts; Dust Bowl migrants; politics
description: Hudson discusses her family's steady employment during the Depression, her teaching salary of $1800 a year, pay cuts in the mid-1930s, and Dust Bowl migrants arriving from the Dakotas and Kansas. She also notes Idaho's Republican politics and her own modest campaigning.

title: World War II; Japanese-American student; air raid drills; husband's illness
description: She recalls taking over a college history class during World War II, defending a Japanese-American student who had been driven from the University of Idaho, and running air raid drills with schoolchildren. The interview closes with her husband's illness and death from cancer and her care for him.

title: Husband's death; return to teaching; apartment move
description: Gertrude Hudson recounts her husband's final illness and death, then explains how she returned to teaching fifth and sixth grade shortly after. She describes finding her current apartment in October 1956 and dealing with building maintenance issues.

title: Apartment furnishings; antiques and furniture
description: Hudson shows the interviewer her antique furniture including a desk from her mother's home, a music cabinet, teakwood pieces from Thailand, and a rosewood set. She explains the origins and craftsmanship of these items.

title: Women's independence; telephone work; rural values
description: Hudson discusses feeling free as a woman and her family's encouragement of independence. She reminisces about the old telephone operator system, learning switchboard work from a friend, and handling a flood emergency. She explains her preference for small-town life over cities.

title: Other work experiences; grocery and hardware stores
description: Hudson describes non-teaching jobs包括 running a friend's grocery store in Spokane and working at a hardware store in Arizona during summer school.

title: Hobbies; travel; homecoming
description: She details her daily routine of checking weather, playing cards, and substitute teaching. Hudson recounts extensive travels to Europe, Alaska, Scandinavia, and the South Pacific, emphasizing that the best part of traveling is returning home to family.

title: Family structure; niece; childless choice
description: Hudson discusses her close-knit family, her brothers' marriages, and her choice not to have children. She describes treating her students and friends' children as her own, including buying a bicycle for her niece.

title: Advice for living; frugality; landlord experience
description: Hudson offers advice on health and following the Golden Rule, criticizing modern materialism and credit card debt. She mentions being a landlord in her previous house and selling it to move to her current apartment.

title: Tomboy childhood; competing with boys
description: Hudson describes growing up as the only girl among boys, her brother training her in baseball and other sports, and maintaining this competitive equality with men throughout her life. She contrasts her experience with other girls who played traditional feminine roles.

title: Reflections on life; financial philosophy
description: Hudson considers whether she would have married younger or continued her education, ultimately valuing the independence she had during the Depression. She emphasizes her belief in paying cash, avoiding debt, and living within one's means.

title: Women's opportunities; faith in God
description: Hudson concludes by stating her belief that women have had chances to express themselves, though some have been dominated by men, and affirms her faith in God and in human nature.
